title: Why rain smells good
hook: That fresh smell after a storm has a real name.

screens.heading: That fresh smell
screens.body: After rain, the air sometimes smells clean and earthy. People love that smell. It even has a name: petrichor. Say it like this: PET-ri-kor.

petrichor.meaning: The earthy smell when rain hits dry ground.
petrichor.example: Like when you step outside after a summer storm and breathe in deep.

screens.heading: Dry ground waits
screens.body: Before rain falls, the ground can be dry and dusty. Tiny bits of soil and plants sit on the surface. They wait quietly until raindrops arrive.

screens.heading: Tiny helpers in soil
screens.body: Soil holds tiny living things called bacteria. Some make an oil that soaks into the ground. The oil can sit there a long time without you noticing.

bacteria.meaning: Very tiny living things — too small to see without a microscope.
bacteria.example: They help soil stay healthy, kind of like tiny garden helpers.

screens.heading: Raindrops splash up
screens.body: When a raindrop hits the ground, it splashes. That splash sends tiny droplets into the air. Those droplets carry the oil smell upward to your nose.

screens.heading: Wind brings it to you
screens.body: A little breeze can carry the smell across a yard or street. That is why you sometimes smell rain before you get wet. Your nose catches it first.

screens.heading: Notice next time
screens.body: Next time it rains, pause for ten seconds. Breathe in slowly. Can you smell petrichor? You are noticing real science — like a curious explorer.

petrichor.meaning: The earthy smell when rain hits dry ground.
petrichor.example: Try smelling the air right after rain on a sidewalk.
